subject: Income-tax Law
question_html: Which of the following correctly describes the sequence in arriving at 'Total Income' as understood under the Income-tax Act, 2025?

options.A: Income is first classified and computed under five heads of income; the aggregate of income under each head is 'Gross Total Income'; deductions are then claimed from Gross Total Income to arrive at 'Total Income'
options.B: 'Total Income' and 'Gross Total Income' are identical terms used interchangeably, with no deductions ever being claimed between the two stages
options.C: Total Income is computed first, and Gross Total Income is derived afterwards by adding back all deductions claimed
options.D: Income is classified under three heads only, and Gross Total Income is arrived at directly without any aggregation of head-wise income

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Income is first classified and computed under five heads of income; the aggregate of income under each head is 'Gross Total Income'; deductions are then claimed from Gross Total Income to arrive at 'Total Income'

Income of an assessee is classified and computed under five heads. The aggregate is Gross Total Income. Certain deductions are then allowed from Gross Total Income, and the resulting figure is Total Income.

question_html: Which of the following correctly reflects how different categories of assessees are classified on the basis of residential status?

options.A: All categories of assessees, without exception, are classified into the same three categories used for individuals and HUFs
options.B: Individuals and HUFs are classified into three categories - resident and ordinarily resident, resident but not ordinarily resident, and non-resident - whereas all other assessees (firms, AOPs, BOIs, companies, local authorities, and artificial juridical persons) are classified into only two categories - resident and non-resident

question_html: Under the general basic conditions of section 6(2) (before considering any relaxation), an individual is resident in India in a tax year if he satisfies which of the following?

options.A: He has been in India for 182 days or more in that tax year AND for 60 days or more in each of the 4 years immediately preceding that tax year, both conditions being mandatory
options.B: He has been in India for 90 days or more in that tax year, with no reference whatsoever to his stay in preceding years
options.C: He has been in India for 365 days or more cumulatively at any point during his lifetime, regardless of the specific tax year under consideration
options.D: He has been in India for a period of 182 days or more in that tax year, OR he has been in India for 60 days or more during that tax year AND for 365 days or more cumulatively in the 4 years immediately preceding that tax year

answer_html:

As per section 6(2), an individual is resident in India in a tax year if he satisfies EITHER of the two basic conditions: (i) stay of 182 days or more in that tax year, OR (ii) stay of 60 days or more in that tax year combined with stay of 365 days or more in the 4 years preceding that tax year. Satisfying either condition suffices.

question_html: Ms. Farah stayed in India for 45 days during tax year 2026-27, and for 300 days cumulatively in the 4 years preceding tax year 2026-27. Assuming no relaxation applies, what is her residential status for tax year 2026-27?

question_html: Which of the following correctly describes how an individual's 'stay in India' is computed for residential status purposes?

options.A: The stay must be continuous and at a single, fixed location within India for it to count towards the residential status computation
options.B: Only the date of arrival is counted as a day of stay in India; the date of departure is always excluded from the computation
options.C: The stay need not be continuous or at any particular/usual location within India, and both the date of arrival and the date of departure are counted as days of stay in India

Stay in India for residential status purposes need not be continuous or at a usual location, and both the date of arrival in and date of departure from India are included as days of stay in India. Additionally, presence within Indian territorial waters (within 12 nautical miles of the coastline) also counts as stay in India.

options.B: Resident, since a stay of 150 days satisfies a relaxed 120-day threshold that applies to every citizen or person of Indian origin visiting India, regardless of income

question_html: Which of the following, standing alone, would cause an individual (who is otherwise resident in India for the tax year) to be classified as 'not ordinarily resident' under section 6(13)?

options.A: He has been resident in India in at least 2 out of the 10 tax years preceding the relevant tax year, and has been in India for 730 days or more in the 7 years preceding the relevant tax year (i.e., he satisfies BOTH additional conditions)
options.B: He is a foreign national who has never previously visited India before the relevant tax year, regardless of any other factor
options.C: He has stayed in India for exactly 182 days in the relevant tax year itself, precisely meeting (and not exceeding) the first basic condition
options.D: He has been a non-resident in India in 9 out of the 10 tax years preceding the relevant tax year

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) He has been a non-resident in India in 9 out of the 10 tax years preceding the relevant tax year

Under section 6(13), an individual is 'not ordinarily resident' if he satisfies ANY ONE of the specified conditions, including having been a non-resident in India in 9 out of the 10 tax years preceding the relevant tax year. An individual is resident AND ordinarily resident only if he satisfies BOTH additional conditions (resident in at least 2 of the preceding 10 years, AND in India for 730 days or more in the preceding 7 years).

question_html: Besides the 9-out-of-10-years non-residence test, which other condition, if satisfied, independently renders an otherwise-resident individual 'not ordinarily resident' under section 6(13)?

options.A: He has been in India cumulatively for 729 days or less in the 7 tax years preceding the relevant tax year
options.B: He has been in India cumulatively for 730 days or more in the 7 tax years preceding the relevant tax year
options.C: He has filed his income-tax return in a country other than India for at least one of the preceding 5 tax years
options.D: He has changed his employer more than twice during the 7 tax years preceding the relevant tax year

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) He has been in India cumulatively for 729 days or less in the 7 tax years preceding the relevant tax year

Section 6(13) provides that an individual is not ordinarily resident if he satisfies EITHER of two independent conditions: (i) non-resident in 9 out of the preceding 10 tax years, OR (ii) in India cumulatively for 729 days or less in the preceding 7 tax years. Satisfying either condition alone is sufficient to render him RNOR.

question_html: Mr. Naresh is resident in India for tax year 2026-27. He has been resident in India in 3 out of the 10 tax years preceding 2026-27, and has been in India for 650 days cumulatively in the 7 tax years preceding 2026-27. What is his correct classification?

options.A: Resident and ordinarily resident, since satisfying at least one of the two additional conditions (the 2-out-of-10-years test) is sufficient for ROR classification
options.B: Resident but not ordinarily resident; although he satisfies the 'resident in at least 2 of the preceding 10 years' condition, he does NOT satisfy the 'in India for 730 days or more in the preceding 7 years' condition (650 days is less than 730 days) - and BOTH additional conditions must be satisfied for ROR status, so failing even one makes him RNOR
options.C: Non-resident, since 650 days falls short of the 730-day threshold, and this shortfall alone is sufficient to override his already-established resident status entirely
options.D: Resident and ordinarily resident, since the 650-day stay, though below 730 days, still comfortably exceeds the alternative 729-day RNOR threshold

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Resident but not ordinarily resident; although he satisfies the 'resident in at least 2 of the preceding 10 years' condition, he does NOT satisfy the 'in India for 730 days or more in the preceding 7 years' condition (650 days is less than 730 days) - and BOTH additional conditions must be satisfied for ROR status, so failing even one makes him RNOR

For ROR status, BOTH additional conditions under section 6(13) must be satisfied cumulatively: resident in at least 2 of the preceding 10 tax years, AND in India for 730 days or more in the preceding 7 tax years. Mr. Naresh fails the second condition (650 days < 730 days), so despite satisfying the first, he is classified as RNOR, not ROR.

question_html: What is the residential sub-classification (ROR or RNOR) applicable to an individual who is a deemed resident under section 6(7)?

question_html: What does 'control and management' mean for the purposes of determining an HUF's residential status?

options.A: The place where the HUF's day-to-day business operations and transactions are physically carried out by employees or agents, regardless of who takes overall policy decisions
options.B: De facto control and management (not merely the right to control or manage), referring to the central control and management of the HUF's affairs, and not to the carrying on of day-to-day business by servants, employees, or agents - i.e., the place where 'the head and brain' of the venture is situated
options.C: The registered address of the HUF as recorded with the jurisdictional Assessing Officer, regardless of where actual decision-making occurs

The place of control may differ from the usual place of running the business, and even from the registered office; it is the place where the 'head and brain' of the enterprise is situated.

question_html: An HUF's day-to-day trading operations are physically carried out entirely by employees based in Mumbai, but every major policy decision (investment strategy, expansion, senior appointments) is taken personally by the Karta while he is in London, where he permanently resides. Where is the HUF's control and management situated?

options.A: In Mumbai; since day-to-day trading operations are physically conducted there, this location conclusively determines the HUF's control and management, regardless of where high-level policy decisions are actually made
options.B: The control and management is necessarily situated partly in India and partly outside India whenever both day-to-day operations and policy decisions occur in different countries, without exception
options.C: In London; since control and management refers to the central control and management (where the 'head and brain' resides, i.e., where policy decisions are actually made by the Karta) and not to the carrying on of day-to-day business by employees, the HUF's control and management would be regarded as situated wholly outside India, notwithstanding that day-to-day operations occur in Mumbai
options.D: The question is indeterminate as a matter of law, since the Income-tax Act, 2025 does not provide any test for ascertaining the location of control and management of an HUF

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) In London; since control and management refers to the central control and management (where the 'head and brain' resides, i.e., where policy decisions are actually made by the Karta) and not to the carrying on of day-to-day business by employees, the HUF's control and management would be regarded as situated wholly outside India, notwithstanding that day-to-day operations occur in Mumbai

The business may be carried on from a location (e.g., Mumbai, via employees), yet control and management may still be situated wholly elsewhere (e.g., London), if that is where actual policy/strategic decisions are made by the Karta. question_html: An HUF, resident in India for the tax year (control and management partly in India), has a Karta who has been a non-resident in India in 9 out of the 10 tax years preceding that tax year. What is the HUF's residential status?

options.B: Resident and ordinarily resident, since the HUF itself (as opposed to its Karta) is resident in India for the current tax year, which alone is treated as sufficient for ROR status

Where an HUF is resident, its further classification as ROR or RNOR is determined by testing the Karta against the same additional conditions applicable to individuals under section 6(13). If the Karta satisfies either the 9-out-of-10-years-non-resident test or the 729-days-or-less-in-7-years test, the HUF is RNOR.

options.A: It is an Indian company AND its place of effective management in that year is in India, both conditions being mandatory and cumulative

question_html: An RNOR individual carries on a business that is controlled from Delhi, but a portion of the profits of this business accrues in Singapore and is neither received nor deemed to be received in India. Is this Singapore-sourced business income included in his total income?

options.A: No; an RNOR is never taxed on any income that accrues outside India, without exception, regardless of whether the underlying business is controlled from India or from abroad
options.B: Yes; although as a general rule an RNOR is not taxed on income accruing outside India (unless received/deemed received in India), a specific exception applies to income derived from a business controlled in India (or a profession set up in India) - such income IS included in the RNOR's total income even though it accrues outside India
options.C: Yes, but only to the extent of 50% of such foreign-accrued business income, this being a specific statutory concession applicable uniquely to RNOR assessees

Correct answer: (B) Yes; although as a general rule an RNOR is not taxed on income accruing outside India (unless received/deemed received in India), a specific exception applies to income derived from a business controlled in India (or a profession set up in India) - such income IS included in the RNOR's total income even though it accrues outside India

The scope of total income for an RNOR specifically includes income accruing or arising outside India where it is derived from a business controlled in India or a profession set up in India - this is the key distinguishing feature of RNOR scope as against non-resident scope (where no such exception applies).

subject: Income-tax Law
question_html: A non-resident individual runs a business that is controlled entirely from outside India, and a portion of its profits accrues outside India and is not received or deemed to be received in India. Is this foreign-accrued business income included in his total income?

options.A: Yes; the business-controlled-in-India exception that applies to RNOR individuals applies with equal force to non-residents, so such income would be included regardless of where the business is controlled from
options.B: Yes, but only if the non-resident subsequently visits India for at least 30 days within the same tax year, this visit being treated as sufficient nexus to bring the foreign income to tax
options.C: No; a non-resident's total income includes only income received or deemed to be received in India, and income accruing/arising or deemed to accrue/arise in India - the special business-controlled-in-India exception available to RNOR individuals is NOT extended to non-residents (and, in any event, here the business itself is controlled from outside India, not from India)
options.D: No, but only because the specific business happens to be controlled from outside India; had it been controlled from India, non-resident status alone would still not extend the scope of his total income to cover such foreign-accrued income

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) No; a non-resident's total income includes only income received or deemed to be received in India, and income accruing/arising or deemed to accrue/arise in India - the special business-controlled-in-India exception available to RNOR individuals is NOT extended to non-residents (and, in any event, here the business itself is controlled from outside India, not from India)

A non-resident's total income comprises only income received/deemed received in India and income accrued/arisen/deemed to accrue or arise in India - there is no extension to income accruing outside India, even if derived from a business controlled in India (that specific extension applies only to RNOR, not to non-residents).

question_html: Which category of income is included in the total income of a resident and ordinarily resident, a resident but not ordinarily resident, AND a non-resident, alike (i.e., regardless of residential status)?

options.A: Income accruing or arising outside India from any source, regardless of its connection (or lack thereof) with a business or profession controlled or set up in India
options.B: Only income received in India, to the exclusion of income that is merely deemed to be received in India, deemed accrual being relevant only for resident assessees
options.C: No category of income is common to all three - each of the three residential status categories has an entirely distinct and non-overlapping scope of total income

question_html: Mr. Faisal, a non-resident seafarer, renders services outside India on a foreign-going ship and receives his salary directly into his NRE (Non-Resident External) account maintained with an Indian bank. As per the relevant CBDT clarification, is this salary income included in his total income?

options.A: No; as clarified by CBDT Circular No. 13/2017 (dated 11.04.2017) and Circular No. 17/2017 (dated 26.04.2017), salary received by a non-resident seafarer for services rendered outside India on a foreign-going ship, credited to an NRE account maintained with an Indian bank, shall NOT be included in total income - it is not treated as 'received in India' merely because the bank account happens to be maintained in India

options.C: No, but only if the seafarer additionally holds a valid Continuous Discharge Certificate demonstrating that his voyage qualifies as an 'eligible voyage' under Rule 8
options.D: Yes, but only to the extent of 50% of the salary so credited, with the balance 50% being exempt under the specific CBDT Circulars referenced above

Correct answer: (A) No; as clarified by CBDT Circular No. 13/2017 (dated 11.04.2017) and Circular No. 17/2017 (dated 26.04.2017), salary received by a non-resident seafarer for services rendered outside India on a foreign-going ship, credited to an NRE account maintained with an Indian bank, shall NOT be included in total income - it is not treated as 'received in India' merely because the bank account happens to be maintained in India

question_html: An individual has dividend income of Rs. 8,000 from an Indian company, received directly in a bank account in London, and never remitted to India. In which of the three residential status categories (ROR/RNOR/Non-resident) would this dividend be included in total income?

options.A: Only for an ROR, since income received outside India (even if deemed to accrue in India) is excluded from the total income of both RNOR and non-resident assessees without exception
options.B: In ALL three categories (ROR, RNOR, and Non-resident) - since dividend paid by an Indian company is deemed to accrue or arise in India under section 9, it falls within 'income accruing or arising or deemed to accrue or arise in India', which is taxable for every category of assessee, irrespective of residential status and irrespective of where it is actually received
options.C: Only for an ROR and RNOR, since dividend income from an Indian company is treated as falling within the special 'business controlled in India' exception that is unavailable to non-residents
options.D: In none of the three categories, since the dividend was both received and retained entirely outside India, with no remittance to India at any point

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) In ALL three categories (ROR, RNOR, and Non-resident) - since dividend paid by an Indian company is deemed to accrue or arise in India under section 9, it falls within 'income accruing or arising or deemed to accrue or arise in India', which is taxable for every category of assessee, irrespective of residential status and irrespective of where it is actually received

Dividend paid by an Indian company (even if paid/received outside India) is deemed to accrue or arise in India under section 9(4). Since income deemed to accrue or arise in India is taxable for every category of assessee (ROR, RNOR, and non-resident) regardless of residential status, this dividend is included in total income in all three cases.

question_html: What is the distinction between income 'accruing' and income becoming 'due', as illustrated by interest on Government securities payable on specified dates (say, 1st January and 1st July)?

options.A: 'Accrue' and 'due' are synonymous terms describing the exact same point in time, namely the date on which payment is actually enforceable by the recipient
options.B: 'Due' refers to the day-to-day vesting of the right to receive income, while 'accrue' refers to the specific date on which payment becomes legally enforceable - i.e., the reverse of the correct distinction
options.C: 'Accrue' refers to the right to receive income, which arises day-to-day over the holding period (e.g., interest accrues from 1st July to 31st December), whereas 'due' refers to the right to enforce payment, which arises only on the specified payment date (e.g., interest falls due for payment on 1st January)
options.D: Neither term has any independent legal significance under the Income-tax Act, 2025; only the date of actual physical receipt of income is ever relevant for taxability

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) 'Accrue' refers to the right to receive income, which arises day-to-day over the holding period (e.g., interest accrues from 1st July to 31st December), whereas 'due' refers to the right to enforce payment, which arises only on the specified payment date (e.g., interest falls due for payment on 1st January)

'Accrue' refers to the right to receive income (arising day-to-day, as the right vests), while 'due' refers to the right to enforce payment of that income (arising on the specified date). For example, salary for December accrues day-to-day through the month but becomes due only when the salary bill is passed.

subject: Income-tax Law
question_html: An item of income has already been included in an assessee's total income on the basis that it accrued or arose (or was deemed to accrue or arise) to him. Can this same item of income subsequently be included again in his total income on the basis that it was later received (or deemed to be received) by him?

options.A: Yes; income must always be taxed twice - once on an accrual basis and again on a receipt basis - to ensure comprehensive coverage under the Income-tax Act, 2025
options.B: Yes, but only where the assessee is a company; for individuals and HUFs, income is taxed only once, either on accrual or receipt basis, but never both
options.C: No, but only if the assessee has changed his method of accounting between the two points in time; if the method of accounting remains unchanged, both taxation events are valid
options.D: No; once an item of income is included in the total income on the basis of accrual/arising (or deemed accrual/arising), it cannot again be included in total income on the basis that it is later received or deemed to be received - this would amount to double taxation of the same income

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) No; once an item of income is included in the total income on the basis of accrual/arising (or deemed accrual/arising), it cannot again be included in total income on the basis that it is later received or deemed to be received - this would amount to double taxation of the same income

Income taxed on an accrual basis cannot be assessed again on a receipt basis (or vice versa), as this would amount to double taxation of the same income. Once included on one basis, the same item is not included again merely because it is subsequently received.

question_html: Which of the following is specifically covered under 'income deemed to be received' as per section 7(1)?

options.A: Interest credited in excess of the notified rate per annum on the balance to the credit of an employee's Recognised Provident Fund account, being the annual accretion (comprising the employer's contribution and interest thereon transferred from an unrecognised provident fund to a recognised provident fund)
options.B: Any salary income that is credited to an employee's bank account on the last working day of a calendar month, regardless of whether it relates to a recognised or unrecognised provident fund
options.C: Dividend income declared by an Indian company but not yet actually paid or credited to the shareholder's account, this being treated as deemed receipt purely by virtue of the declaration itself
options.D: Rental income accrued on a house property but not yet actually received by the landlord from the tenant, treated as deemed receipt purely by virtue of accrual

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Interest credited in excess of the notified rate per annum on the balance to the credit of an employee's Recognised Provident Fund account, being the annual accretion (comprising the employer's contribution and interest thereon transferred from an unrecognised provident fund to a recognised provident fund)

Section 7(1) deems certain amounts to be 'received' even without actual receipt, including: annual accretion (employer's contribution and interest) to a recognised provident fund transferred from an unrecognised fund, in excess of the specified/notified threshold; contribution by the Central Government or any other employer to the account of an employee under a specified pension scheme; and amounts transferred from a scheme referred to under section 124.

question_html: As per section 9(2), income accruing or arising to an assessee outside India (whether directly or indirectly) would be deemed to accrue or arise in India if it arises through or from which of the following?

question_html: A foreign lessee pays hire charges outside India to an Indian lessor for the use of machinery physically situated in India. Are these hire charges deemed to accrue or arise in India?

options.A: No; since the hire charges are paid outside India, they are treated as arising entirely outside India and are therefore not deemed to accrue or arise in India under any circumstances
options.B: Yes, but only if the lessee is also an Indian resident; where the lessee is a foreign person, hire charges for Indian-situated machinery are not deemed to accrue or arise in India

question_html: A non-resident transfers shares of an Indian company while physically present in Singapore, and receives the entire sale consideration in Dubai. Are the resulting capital gains deemed to accrue or arise in India?

options.A: No; since both the transfer transaction (in Singapore) and the receipt of consideration (in Dubai) occurred entirely outside India, the capital gains cannot be deemed to accrue or arise in India under any circumstances
options.B: Yes, but only if the transfer document was registered in India, this registration being an essential precondition under section 9(2) for capital gains on transfer of an Indian capital asset to be deemed to accrue or arise in India
options.C: No, unless the non-resident subsequently remits the sale proceeds into India within the same tax year, such remittance being necessary to trigger deemed accrual under section 9(2)
options.D: Yes; capital gains arising through or from the transfer of a capital asset situated in India are deemed to accrue or arise in India in all cases, irrespective of whether the asset is movable or immovable, tangible or intangible, irrespective of the place of registration of the transfer document, and irrespective of the place of payment of consideration

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) Yes; capital gains arising through or from the transfer of a capital asset situated in India are deemed to accrue or arise in India in all cases, irrespective of whether the asset is movable or immovable, tangible or intangible, irrespective of the place of registration of the transfer document, and irrespective of the place of payment of consideration

Section 9(2) deems capital gains from transfer of a capital asset situated in India to accrue or arise in India in ALL cases - irrespective of the nature of the asset, the place of registration of the transfer document, or the place of payment of consideration. Neither the place of transfer nor the place of receipt of consideration is determinative.

question_html: Mr. Xavier, resident in New York, USA, owns a house property situated in India, which he has let out on rent. Is the rent taxable in India?

options.A: Yes; rent receivable/received by Mr. Xavier would be taxable in India, whether such rent is received by him in India or outside India, since the house property itself is situated in India
options.B: No; since Mr. Xavier himself resides outside India (in New York), any rental income he earns is treated as entirely foreign-sourced and outside the scope of Indian taxation
options.C: Yes, but only if the rent is actually received within India; rent received outside India in respect of an India-situated property is never taxable in India
options.D: No, unless the tenant occupying the property is also a non-resident; rent from a resident tenant occupying an India-situated property owned by a non-resident is exempt

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Yes; rent receivable/received by Mr. Xavier would be taxable in India, whether such rent is received by him in India or outside India, since the house property itself is situated in India

Since the house property is situated in India, income (rent) arising from it is deemed to accrue or arise in India, and is taxable in India regardless of where Mr. Xavier resides and regardless of whether the rent is actually received in India or outside India.

question_html: A non-resident maintains a purchasing office in India solely to purchase goods in India for the purpose of exporting them out of India, with no other activity carried out in India. Does this activity constitute a 'business connection' in India, deeming income to accrue or arise in India?

options.A: Yes; any physical presence of a non-resident's office in India, for whatever purpose, automatically constitutes a business connection in India and results in deemed accrual of income
options.B: No, but only if the non-resident additionally proves that the goods so purchased are exported within 90 days of purchase, this time limit being a specific statutory condition
options.C: No; purchase of goods in India for the purpose of export out of India is specifically excluded from constituting business carried out in India, and therefore does not give rise to income deemed to accrue or arise in India under section 9(9)(c)
options.D: Yes, but only to the extent of 10% of the value of goods purchased, this percentage being deemed attributable to Indian operations regardless of the export-purchase exclusion

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) No; purchase of goods in India for the purpose of export out of India is specifically excluded from constituting business carried out in India, and therefore does not give rise to income deemed to accrue or arise in India under section 9(9)(c)

Section 9(9)(c) specifically excludes 'purchase of goods in India for the purpose of export out of India' from constituting business carried out in India - this activity does not, by itself, create a business connection or result in deemed accrual of income in India.

question_html: Which of the following non-residents, shooting a cinematograph film in India, would benefit from the specific exclusion from 'business carried out in India' under section 9(9)(c)?

options.A: An individual non-resident who is not a citizen of India (or a firm with no partner who is an Indian citizen/Indian resident, or a company with no shareholder who is an Indian citizen/Indian resident)
options.B: Any non-resident whatsoever, regardless of citizenship, so long as the film being shot is intended exclusively for exhibition outside India
options.C: An Indian citizen who is permanently settled and tax-resident outside India, shooting a film in India for a foreign production house
options.D: A foreign company, even where one of its shareholders is an Indian citizen or an Indian resident, so long as the majority of shareholders are foreign nationals

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) An individual non-resident who is not a citizen of India (or a firm with no partner who is an Indian citizen/Indian resident, or a company with no shareholder who is an Indian citizen/Indian resident)

Shooting of a cinematograph film in India is excluded from constituting business carried out in India where the non-resident is: (a) an individual who is NOT a citizen of India, (b) a firm with no partner who is a citizen of India or resident in India, or (c) a company with no shareholder who is a citizen of India or resident in India. question_html: Which categories of salary income are deemed to accrue or arise in India under section 9(3)(a)?

options.A: Only salary that is actually paid or disbursed within Indian territory, regardless of where the underlying employment services were physically rendered
options.B: Salary earned in India for services rendered in India, and salary for a rest period or leave period which is both preceded and succeeded by services rendered in India and forms part of the service contract of employment

question_html: Salary payable by the Government of India to a citizen of India for services rendered OUTSIDE India is:

options.A: Never taxable in India, since services rendered entirely outside India are, as a general principle, always excluded from the scope of Indian salary taxation regardless of the identity of the employer
options.B: Taxable in India only if the citizen is also resident in India for that tax year; for a non-resident citizen, such Government salary is entirely exempt from Indian taxation
options.C: Deemed to accrue or arise in India under section 9(3)(b), and is therefore taxable in India, notwithstanding that the services were rendered entirely outside India

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Deemed to accrue or arise in India under section 9(3)(b), and is therefore taxable in India, notwithstanding that the services were rendered entirely outside India

As per section 9(3)(b), salary payable by the Government to a citizen of India for services rendered OUTSIDE India is specifically deemed to accrue or arise in India - and is therefore taxable in India even though the recipient may be a non-resident and the services were rendered abroad.

question_html: A dividend is declared and paid by an Indian company to its shareholder entirely outside India. Is this dividend deemed to accrue or arise in India?

question_html: Under section 9(5), interest payable by a NON-RESIDENT is deemed to accrue or arise in India only if:

options.A: The lender to whom such interest is paid happens to be an Indian citizen, regardless of the purpose for which the underlying debt or borrowed money is used
options.B: The debt was incurred, or the money borrowed, is used for the purposes of a business or profession carried on by such non-resident IN India

question_html: Mr. A, a non-resident, borrows money from Mr. B, another non-resident, and invests the borrowed money in shares of an Indian company (a portfolio investment, not a business carried on by Mr. A in India). Is the interest payable by Mr. A to Mr. B deemed to accrue or arise in India?

options.A: Yes; since the money was ultimately invested in shares of an Indian company, the interest payable is automatically deemed to accrue or arise in India, regardless of whether this investment constitutes a business carried on in India by Mr. A
options.B: Yes; interest payable between two non-residents is always deemed to accrue or arise in India, regardless of the location or purpose for which the borrowed funds are applied
options.C: No; interest payable by a non-resident (Mr. A) is deemed to accrue or arise in India only if the money borrowed is used for the purposes of a business or profession carried on by that non-resident IN India - since Mr. A merely made a portfolio investment in shares (not a business carried on in India), the interest payable to Mr. B is NOT deemed to accrue or arise in India
options.D: No, but only because both parties (Mr. A and Mr. B) are non-residents; had either party been a resident of India, the interest would automatically be deemed to accrue or arise in India

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) No; interest payable by a non-resident (Mr. A) is deemed to accrue or arise in India only if the money borrowed is used for the purposes of a business or profession carried on by that non-resident IN India - since Mr. A merely made a portfolio investment in shares (not a business carried on in India), the interest payable to Mr. B is NOT deemed to accrue or arise in India

As specifically illustrated in the Study Material, if a non-resident 'A' borrows money from a non-resident 'B' and merely invests it in shares of an Indian company (not carrying on a business in India), interest payable by A to B will NOT be deemed to accrue or arise in India. subject: Income-tax Law
case_facts_html: Mr. Rizwan, a non-resident, borrows funds from a bank in the UK and uses the entire borrowed amount for his own manufacturing business carried on through a branch in Pune, India, paying interest to the UK bank. Separately, ABC Ltd., an Indian resident company, pays royalty to Yamato Corp, a Japanese company, for the use of a patent that is utilised exclusively at ABC Ltd.'s factory in Germany.
question_html: Is the interest paid by Mr. Rizwan (a non-resident) to the UK bank deemed to accrue or arise in India?

options.A: No; since both Mr. Rizwan and the UK bank are situated outside India, the interest payable between them can never be deemed to accrue or arise in India, regardless of how the borrowed funds are used
options.B: Yes; interest payable by a non-resident is deemed to accrue or arise in India where the money borrowed is used for the purposes of a business or profession carried on by that non-resident IN India - here, Mr. Rizwan used the borrowed funds for his own manufacturing business carried on through a branch in Pune, India
options.C: Yes, but only because the lender is a bank rather than an individual; interest payable to a non-bank non-resident lender would not be deemed to accrue or arise in India even on identical facts
options.D: No, unless the loan agreement is specifically registered with an Indian regulatory authority, this registration being a mandatory precondition for deemed accrual

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Yes; interest payable by a non-resident is deemed to accrue or arise in India where the money borrowed is used for the purposes of a business or profession carried on by that non-resident IN India - here, Mr. Rizwan used the borrowed funds for his own manufacturing business carried on through a branch in Pune, India

Interest payable by a non-resident is deemed to accrue or arise in India specifically where the debt/borrowed money is used for a business or profession carried on by that non-resident IN India. Since Mr. Rizwan used the UK bank's funds for his manufacturing business in Pune, the interest is deemed to accrue or arise in India.

subject: Income-tax Law
case_facts_html: Mr. Rizwan, a non-resident, borrows funds from a bank in the UK and uses the entire borrowed amount for his own manufacturing business carried on through a branch in Pune, India, paying interest to the UK bank. Separately, ABC Ltd., an Indian resident company, pays royalty to Yamato Corp, a Japanese company, for the use of a patent that is utilised exclusively at ABC Ltd.'s factory in Germany.
question_html: Is the royalty paid by ABC Ltd. (a resident) to Yamato Corp deemed to accrue or arise in India, given that the patent is utilised exclusively at ABC Ltd.'s factory in Germany?

options.A: Yes; royalty payable by any Indian resident company to a foreign company is always deemed to accrue or arise in India, regardless of where the underlying right or property is actually utilised
options.B: Yes, but only to the extent of 50% of the royalty amount, this being a specific statutory apportionment applicable to cross-border royalty payments used partly outside India
options.C: No; royalty payable by a resident is deemed to accrue or arise in India EXCEPT where it is payable for a right/property utilised for the purposes of a business carried on by such resident OUTSIDE India - since ABC Ltd.'s use of the patent is exclusively for its Germany factory (a business carried on outside India), this specific exception applies, and the royalty is not deemed to accrue or arise in India
options.D: No, but only because Yamato Corp is a Japanese company; had the recipient been resident in a country with which India has no double taxation avoidance agreement, the royalty would have been deemed to accrue or arise in India

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) No; royalty payable by a resident is deemed to accrue or arise in India EXCEPT where it is payable for a right/property utilised for the purposes of a business carried on by such resident OUTSIDE India - since ABC Ltd.'s use of the patent is exclusively for its Germany factory (a business carried on outside India), this specific exception applies, and the royalty is not deemed to accrue or arise in India

Royalty payable by a resident is deemed to accrue or arise in India EXCEPT where payable for a right/property used for a business carried on by such resident OUTSIDE India (or for earning income from a source outside India). Since ABC Ltd.'s patent use is exclusively for its Germany factory, this exception applies and the royalty is not deemed to accrue or arise in India.

case_facts_html: Mr. Rizwan, a non-resident, borrows funds from a bank in the UK and uses the entire borrowed amount for his own manufacturing business carried on through a branch in Pune, India, paying interest to the UK bank. Separately, ABC Ltd., an Indian resident company, pays royalty to Yamato Corp, a Japanese company, for the use of a patent that is utilised exclusively at ABC Ltd.'s factory in Germany.
question_html: Suppose, instead, ABC Ltd.'s patent were utilised exclusively at its Chennai factory in India (rather than at a factory in Germany). Would the royalty payable to Yamato Corp then be deemed to accrue or arise in India, and would this affect its taxability irrespective of any territorial nexus considerations?

options.A: No; royalty payments to a foreign company are never deemed to accrue or arise in India, regardless of where the underlying right or property is utilised by the Indian payer
options.B: Yes, but only if Yamato Corp also maintains a registered office in India, this being an independent and additional precondition under section 9(11) for taxability of royalty income
options.C: No; taxability under section 9(11) would still be excluded here since Yamato Corp itself has no business connection or presence in India, regardless of where ABC Ltd. utilises the patent
options.D: Yes; since the patent would now be utilised for a business carried on by ABC Ltd. WITHIN India, the specific 'business carried on outside India' exception would no longer apply, and the royalty would be deemed to accrue or arise in India - further, under section 9(11), this would be taxable in Yamato Corp's hands irrespective of whether Yamato Corp has any residence, place of business, or business connection in India, or whether any services were rendered in India

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) Yes; since the patent would now be utilised for a business carried on by ABC Ltd. WITHIN India, the specific 'business carried on outside India' exception would no longer apply, and the royalty would be deemed to accrue or arise in India - further, under section 9(11), this would be taxable in Yamato Corp's hands irrespective of whether Yamato Corp has any residence, place of business, or business connection in India, or whether any services were rendered in India

If the patent were utilised for ABC Ltd.'s business carried on within India (Chennai), the exception for business carried on outside India would not apply, and the royalty would be deemed to accrue or arise in India. Under section 9(11), such royalty is taxable in the non-resident recipient's hands irrespective of territorial nexus - i.e., irrespective of whether Yamato Corp has any residence, place of business, or business connection in India.
